messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Tran, a 60-year-old South Eastern Asian fisherman, has been struggling with the aftermath of an event that forever altered his perception of safety and trust. About six months ago, during a routine fishing trip, Mr. Tran witnessed the tragic loss of one of his crew members when their boat capsized in heavy waves. The memory of that day is vivid for him; he still sees the panic on his colleague's face as they were swept away by the turbulent sea. Since then, Mr. Tran has experienced strong physical reactions whenever something reminds him of that stressful experience. Even the sound of rough water or the sight of a stormy sky sends waves of fear through him. These triggers are potent because he vividly recalls the terrifying moment when their boat capsized and his colleague vanished beneath the surface. Mr. Tran's fears have only deepened over time, as he has come to believe that people cannot be trusted. The thought that such an event could happen again, and that those around him might not care or be able to help, exacerbates his anxiety. His mistrust is a direct consequence of these strong negative feelings; every wave, every storm cloud, triggers intense fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame. He has also experienced significant emotional numbness since the accident. He often feels as though he’s walking through life in a haze, unable to connect deeply with his surroundings or even his family. This sense of being dead inside is particularly troubling for him because it makes it difficult to enjoy activities that once brought him joy, like spending time at sea. Mr. Tran's guilt over surviving the accident when others did not has intensified these feelings. He carries a heavy burden of survival guilt, believing he should have done more to save his colleague. This sense of responsibility and remorse has made him increasingly wary and mistrustful of those around him, fearing that they might also be vulnerable or unreliable. The weight of these negative appraisals amplifies Mr. Tran’s threat perception, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where every trigger brings forth stronger physical reactions and deeper emotional turmoil. His trust in others has eroded significantly, leading to increased anxiety and fear about future events. For instance, he often skips fishing trips, fearing that another accident could occur. This pattern of mistrust and heightened threat perception has strained his relationship with his wife and community. He avoids social gatherings and even fishing outings, isolating himself from the very activities and people who once brought him comfort and support. What finally brought Mr. Tran to seek help was a particularly severe episode where he experienced intense physical reactions after a recent storm warning on the local news. The anxiety and guilt became so overwhelming that he realized he could no longer continue living in this state of constant fear and emotional numbness. Mr. Tran is most afraid of not being able to reconnect with his loved ones and facing more traumatic events without support. He hopes for relief from these intense feelings, a way to regain trust in others, and the ability to enjoy life again without the constant burden of guilt and fear.
